lab.protocol: Both weeks average 7 hours of sleep per night. Both balls start at the selected position on the baseline landscape. One stressor of the selected intensity hits both at the same time and in the same direction.
lab.apply: Apply one stressor to both weeks
lab.metric: The final frame shows displacement in model position units and return time in model seconds. Return requires staying within ±0.10 units of the start through the end for at least 0.5 seconds.
lab.assumption: STEP-BD linked sleep variability with symptom severity. We chose lower damping for the variable week as an educational assumption.
lab.caseHint: Fictional five-day case. Explore how two dimensions change from the person’s usual level (0). Scores are illustrative.
lab.axes: Horizontal axis: mood. Vertical axis: activation.
observations: Feels low and struggles to get started with everyday tasks.
Mood drops further. Spends most of the day inactive.
Mood remains low. Daily activity returns to its usual level.
Still feels low. Starts several new projects in one evening.
While still feeling low, works on projects through the night and describes racing thoughts.

interview.title: Clinical interview · A teenager sleeping less during exams
interview.intro: Fictional case. On Friday you see Deniz, 16, with their mother. “It started with the exam and got worse after an argument with a friend.” Explore all three topics and choose an initial assessment.
interview.sequence: Ask Deniz · What happened first this week?
interview.sequenceReply: Deniz: “I studied on Monday. After the exam on Tuesday I was still up late. On Wednesday morning I posted three project ideas to the class chat. I argued with my friend on Thursday.”
interview.sleep: Ask Deniz · How did you feel the next morning?
interview.sleepReply: Deniz: “On Monday I slept three hours and could barely keep my eyes open in the exam. The next two nights I had no studying to do. Four hours felt enough and I woke refreshed. I usually sleep eight.”
interview.function: Ask the mother · What changed at home and school?
interview.functionReply: Mother: “Since Tuesday evening Deniz has been talking much faster. They rearranged their room at midnight. The teacher said they kept speaking up on Wednesday. This is new.”
interview.assess: Which initial assessment would you document?
interview.situational: Exam demands and conflict explain the change.
interview.situationalFeedback: Limited sleep opportunity and fatigue fit the first night. Later, Deniz had time to sleep and felt rested after four hours. Increased activity and rapid speech preceded the argument.
interview.possible: Explore a possible mood episode given reduced need for sleep and new behavioral changes.
interview.possibleFeedback: Best supported. Feeling rested after little sleep coincides with changes reported at home and school. Assess mood quality, duration, impairment, safety and medication or substance use. Ask about earlier episodes and follow the course.
interview.confirmed: The history confirms a manic episode.
interview.confirmedFeedback: An episodic change warrants assessment. Mood quality, total duration, degree of impairment and alternative explanations still need clarification.
interview.source: Source · Assessment of bipolar disorder in children and adolescents

attractorTheory.title: The Landscape and Attractor Model
attractorTheory.description: Bipolar disorder can be modeled as an 'energy landscape' where Mania and Depression are stable basins (attractors). Without treatment, Euthymia (stable mood) is often an unstable point — any stressor can push the system into a pathological state. Lithium works by reshaping this landscape, making euthymia a safe point of balance.

ui.landscapeDescription: Landscape of mania, euthymia and depression. The angry face illustrates irritability that can accompany mania. The sad face represents low mood in depression.
